question_text: Find the orthocentre of the triangle whose vertices are (−5,−7), (13,2), (−5,6).

recall_prompt: Say how you would solve this — say which lines meet at the orthocentre, and how you get each one's slope.

steps.label: Set up the orthocentre
steps.margin_note: First mark. The orthocentre is where the three altitudes meet. An altitude runs through one vertex PERPENDICULAR to the opposite side, so every altitude needs two things: a point and a perpendicular slope.
steps.memory_tip: Altitudes meet at the orthocentre; each is a vertex plus the opposite side's perpendicular.

recall.must_convey: That O(x, y) is taken as the orthocentre, the meeting point of the altitudes.
accept: take O x y as the orthocentre where the altitudes meet
the orthocentre is the intersection of the three altitudes
let O be x comma y and write the three vertices
orthocentre ni O x y ga teesukovali
an altitude goes through a vertex perpendicular to the opposite side

steps.why: Circumcentre and orthocentre are the two points this chapter asks for, and they use DIFFERENT lines: perpendicular bisectors for the circumcentre, altitudes for the orthocentre. Naming which one is wanted keeps the method straight.
common_mistakes: Using perpendicular bisectors, which give the circumcentre instead.
Drawing the altitude through the wrong vertex for the side chosen.

steps.label: Draw the triangle
steps.margin_note: Worth no mark but worth drawing. Two altitudes are enough to fix O — the third passes through the same point on its own. The right-angle mark is the whole definition of an altitude.
steps.memory_tip: Two altitudes are enough — the third is automatic.

recall.must_convey: That a triangle ABC is sketched with two altitudes drawn and their meeting point marked O. Naming the drawing is full credit — it cannot be spoken.
accept: draw the triangle and the two altitudes meeting at O
sketch triangle A B C with altitudes from A and from B
make a diagram showing the altitudes crossing at the orthocentre
triangle geesi rendu altitudes mark cheyyali
draw the triangle with its altitudes

steps.why: An altitude goes through one vertex PERPENDICULAR to the opposite side. Drawing it is how you check you have paired the right vertex with the right side before computing any slope.
common_mistakes: Drawing the perpendicular BISECTOR of a side, which gives the circumcentre instead.
Drawing the altitude to a side that touches the vertex it starts from.

steps.label: First altitude through A
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Three moves in order: slope of the OPPOSITE side, flip-and-negate it for the perpendicular, then the point-slope form through the vertex.
steps.memory_tip: Slope of the OPPOSITE side first, then flip and negate, then point-slope.

recall.must_convey: That the slope of the opposite side is found, negated and inverted, and the altitude through A is written.
accept: find the slope of B C, take minus one over it, and write the line through A
slope of the opposite side then its perpendicular slope then point slope form
the altitude through A is perpendicular to B C
B C slope teesi, perpendicular slope teesi, A gundaa line rayali
this gives the first altitude equation

steps.why: The altitude from A is perpendicular to BC, so its slope is −1/m where m is BC's slope. Getting the opposite side right is the step most often rushed.
common_mistakes: Using the slope of AB or AC instead of the opposite side BC.
Taking the perpendicular slope as −m rather than −1/m.

steps.label: Second altitude through B
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Here the opposite side AC is VERTICAL, so its altitude is horizontal: write y = 2, the y-coordinate of B, with no slope formula at all. Two altitudes are enough — the third passes through their intersection automatically.
steps.memory_tip: A vertical side has a horizontal altitude: write y = the vertex's y-coordinate and use no slope formula.
lines: A(−5, −7) and C(−5, 6) share x = −5, so AC is a VERTICAL line
A vertical side has an altitude that is HORIZONTAL, so its slope is 0
Eq. of horizontal line through B(13, 2) is

recall.must_convey: That AC is vertical, so the altitude through B is the horizontal line y = 2.
accept: A C is vertical, so the altitude through B is horizontal
the altitude through B is y equals two
a vertical side gives a horizontal altitude, so no slope is needed
A C vertical ga undi kabatti altitude horizontal, y equals two
this gives the second altitude equation

steps.why: Two altitudes fix the point. The third is a check, not extra information — all three are concurrent by the theorem.
common_mistakes: Reusing the slope of BC for the second altitude.
Trying −1/m on AC, whose slope is undefined because the side is vertical.

steps.label: Solve the pair
steps.margin_note: The last three marks. Two linear equations, one point. Like the circumcentre, this point may lie outside the triangle when the triangle is obtuse.

recall.must_convey: That solving the two altitude equations gives (−3, 2).
accept: solve the two altitude equations together
use cross multiplication or elimination on one and two
solving the pair gives the orthocentre
rendu altitude equations solve chesthe orthocentre vasthundi
the orthocentre is this point

steps.why: In a right-angled triangle the orthocentre sits exactly on the right-angled vertex, which is a quick sanity check when the numbers look surprising.
common_mistakes: Writing the coordinates the wrong way round.

insider_note: A and C share x = −5, so AC is vertical and its altitude is simply horizontal: y = 2, with no slope formula at all. Reaching for −1/m on a vertical side is where this question is lost.
